short: A protracted naval and proxy conflict that defined late Elizabethan foreign policy.
full:
Beginning in 1585, the Anglo-Spanish War was an undeclared conflict driven by religious differences, commercial rivalry, and English support for Dutch Protestant rebels. Queen Elizabeth I formally allied with the Dutch Republic under the Treaty of Nonsuch, prompting Philip II of Spain to begin preparing an invasion of England. The war was characterized by privateering, devastating naval raids, and proxy conflicts in Ireland, France, and the Netherlands.

While the English secured celebrated victories like the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 and the raid on Cadiz in 1596, the broader war was largely a grinding stalemate. Spanish naval power recovered rapidly, launching further armadas that were thwarted by weather rather than English action. The conflict dragged on until both monarchs had died, placing an immense financial burden on the English state that forced the sale of crown lands and provoked domestic unrest. Peace was finally concluded by James I at the Treaty of London in 1604, restoring the pre-war status quo.
